t: 3218. Minimum Cost for Cutting Cake I
o: Every horizontal line eventually must be cut, and each time we cut it, the cost equals horizontalCut[i] times the current number of vertical pieces (segments), because the line is cut once per vertical strip. Hence expensive lines should be cut early, while the piece count in the other direction is still small — a classic exchange-argument greedy. Example 1: cutting the costly vertical line (cost 5×1) first, then horizontals while piece counts are small, totals 13.
k: Cutting line i costs cost_i × (current number of pieces in the perpendicular direction).
Cut lines in decreasing cost order; ties broken arbitrarily within an orientation.
When costs tie across orientations, either order gives the same total.

a.i: Sort both arrays descending and repeatedly take the globally largest remaining cut. Taking a large cut early multiplies it by fewer perpendicular pieces; an exchange argument shows swapping any two adjacent out-of-order cuts never increases cost. Remaining tails are multiplied by the final piece counts.
s: Maintain hp = vp = 1 (piece counts) and answer 0.
While both arrays have items: take the larger front, add cost × opposite piece count, advance, increment that orientation's count.
Multiply and add whatever remains in each array.

w: This greedy is the standard and optimal solution (identical to the 'minimum cost to cut a stick/board' family). Pitfalls: multiplying by the wrong piece count (a horizontal cut multiplies by vertical pieces), and 32-bit overflow in C++/Java — costs up to 1000 × up to 19 pieces each fits, but use 64-bit accumulators out of habit. Follow-up: prove the exchange argument, or handle the version where each cut's cost depends on current piece length.
